summary:
Public Law 118-186, the "Detection Equipment and Technology Evaluation to Counter the Threat of Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024" (or "DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024"), enacted December 23, 2024 (originating as H.R. 8663), directs the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Directorate to develop enhanced capacity to detect and identify illicit substances present in very low concentrations. Its operative mechanism is an amendment to the enumerated responsibilities of the Under Secretary for Science and Technology under the Homeland Security Act of 2002.

Section 2 amends Section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 182) by making conforming punctuation changes to paragraphs (13) and (14) and adding a new paragraph (15). New paragraph (15) authorizes the Directorate, in coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration, to carry out research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses to improve the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of equipment and reference libraries used by Federal, State, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement for accurate drug detection. It enumerates three focus areas: (A) portable equipment capable of detecting and identifying drugs with minimal or no sample handling; (B) equipment able to separate complex mixtures containing low drug concentrations and high concentrations of cutting agents to enable signature extraction for field identification; and (C) technologies employing machine learning or artificial intelligence (as defined in Section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, 15 U.S.C. 9401) and other techniques to predict whether sample substances are controlled substance analogues or new psychoactive substances not yet in available reference libraries.

Section 3 (codified as a note to 6 U.S.C. 182) imposes two requirements on the Under Secretary in carrying out the new Section 302(15): (1) adherence to the recommendations, guidelines, and best practices of the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) or any successor document; and (2) establishment of research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis priorities based on the latest available information, including specific drugs identified as threats in the latest DHS Homeland Threat Assessment, the latest DEA State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or successor documents.

Section 4 (also codified as a 6 U.S.C. 182 note) is a rule of construction providing that nothing in the Act may be construed to limit the authority of agencies currently managing, overseeing, or otherwise involved in drug equipment and reference libraries.

The Act contains no appropriation and no separate authorization of appropriations; it confers authority and imposes procedural requirements without providing funding. It specifies no delayed effective date or sunset provision.
